## Four questions, then the national numbers {.viz}

![](assets/figures/poll_open.svg){width="100%"}

::: notes
Do this before you show the national bars. Four show-of-hands: used AI at work in the last year; used an AI scribe; worried if no human reviews the output; trust these tools for pediatric care. Then advance.
:::

## They use AI. Almost none trust it for children. {.viz}

![](assets/figures/aap_places.svg){width="100%"}

::: notes
PAS 2025. Punchline is 6%. The room just voted. Point at the gap between “I use it” and “I trust it for children.”
:::

## Three ground rules for today.

:::: {.rules-row}
::: {.box .box-orange}
::: {.box-label}
Invented cases
:::

Every demo patient is made up.
:::
::: {.box .box-purple}
::: {.box-label}
No real notes in ChatGPT
:::

Consumer ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini.

No names, record numbers, or pasted notes.
:::
::: {.box .box-teal}
::: {.box-label}
Verify before you copy
:::

Do not copy a dose or a citation into a note until you have opened the source.
:::
::::

::: notes
Ground rules for the room, not a numbered manifesto. Verbally repeat one line: “No real patient data in consumer tools.” If someone offers a real H&P, stop and point at card 1. Consumer cloud is the problem. Local models wait for the next slide. Card 3: open the paper or the monograph before a number or a citation hits the note.
:::

---

## Where the prompt goes is the privacy question. {.viz}

![](assets/figures/hipaa.svg){width="100%"}

::: notes
This is the clinically actionable privacy slide. Consumer ChatGPT: the prompt leaves the building. OpenEvidence’s HIPAA badge is still a vendor cloud. Local Ollama: the prompt stays on the laptop they already use for the EHR. That is a reasonable path. Hospital BAA tools are the official cloud path.
:::

---

## AI is one word for three jobs. {.viz}

![](assets/figures/three_ais.svg){width="100%"}

::: notes
Ask which kind they have already encountered this month. A score, an alert, and a chatbot are all called AI — that sentence is on the canvas. Left box: PEWS and a febrile-infant pathway. Middle: sepsis alert and a chest X-ray read. Right: a parent letter and an AI scribe. FDA does not regulate “AI as such”; it regulates devices by intended use.
:::

---

## A model that is accurate on adults can still fail on children. {.viz}

![](assets/figures/pediatric_shift.svg){width="100%"}

::: notes
Distribution shift. Vendors often quote AUROC; say the model was accurate on adults so they hear the population, not the metric. The 6% PAS number is a conference abstract. Carry it as a prior, not as a prevalence study.
:::

---

## How AI answers {background-color="#00C4B3" .section-break}

---

## A dose is several tokens, not one number. {.viz}

![](assets/figures/tokens.svg){width="100%"}

::: notes
A dose is several tokens. That is why numeric hallucination is easy and why “just one number” is not a simple object inside the net. The split on the canvas is a cartoon and varies by model. Say that, then move on.
:::

---

## The model guesses the next token. It is not looking up an answer. {.viz}

![](assets/figures/next_token.svg){width="100%"}

::: notes
Spoken takeaway: it predicts plausible text; it is not retrieving a stored answer. Decoder-style LLM: given the tokens so far, score the next one, add it, repeat.
:::

---

## The same 38.5 °C is a workup at 3 weeks and often watch-and-treat at 3 years. {.viz}

![](assets/figures/context_age.svg){width="100%"}

::: notes
This replaces transformer anatomy. 38.5 °C in a 3-week-old is a workup clock. In a 3-year-old it is often watch-and-treat. Models need that context the same way you do. If they ask how attention works, the backup slide is after Q&A.
:::

---

## The usual mistake now is a real paper with the wrong claim. {.viz}

![](assets/figures/hallucinations.svg){width="100%"}

::: notes
Old failure: invented PubMed ID. Usual failure now: a real paper with the wrong claim; a rule set at the start can vanish mid-run; citation links that look like proof. Citations and tool use do not eliminate source verification. Artsi: interpretive error even with real citations.
:::

---

## The jobs to remember are autocomplete, chat, and tools. {.viz}

![](assets/figures/three_eras.svg){width="100%"}

::: notes
The goal is a taxonomy they can keep when the posters change. Autocomplete finishes the next word. Chat is a conversation. Tools look things up or test a result. Product names change quickly; these three jobs are what to remember. Full chronology is in backup if someone wants GPT-2 through Fable.
:::

---

## Sources, limits, and files {background-color="#691F74" .section-break}

Three ways to make an answer easier to inspect.

---

## RAG looks a corpus up, then writes. Gemini Notebook is the best-known example. {.viz}

![](assets/figures/rag.svg){width="100%"}

::: notes
Spell RAG once: retrieval-augmented generation — they have heard the acronym. Point at the corpus card — that is the choice. Gemini Notebook is the best-known example (public PDFs with citation links). Do not claim a measured market share. OpenEvidence and UpToDate are other corpora. Reduces some hallucinations. Does not stop wrong-paper, unsupported synthesis, leftover parametric claims, or citation theater.
:::

---

## These models can test an answer and revise it before responding. {.viz}

![](assets/figures/test_time_compute.svg){width="100%"}

::: {.viz-caption}
The 400 mg maximum is the safety limit. 500 mg exceeds it, so the model revises to 400 mg.
:::

::: notes
Vendors sell extra tokens before the answer — a try, test, revise loop you usually do not see. Left is the 2023 chatbot: first fluent sentence, stop there. Right is o1-class: hidden scratch work, then one answer. The toy is a 10 mg/kg dose that needs a 400 mg maximum: 50 kg × 10 = 500, which fails the maximum, so the revised answer is 400 mg. The line under the boxes is that in English. Coding tests had an automated limit test like that first; keep that history off the canvas unless someone asks. Files and tools are the next slide. o1 Sep 2024; DeepSeek-R1 Jan 2025 if someone asks whether it was OpenAI-only.
:::

---

## A chatbot returns a paragraph. A harness returns a file. {.viz}

![](assets/figures/harness_loop.svg?rev=20260828){width="100%"}

::: notes
Ask: which row produces something another person can inspect tomorrow? Top row is a chatbot: prompt in, a paragraph out, you copy it. Bottom row is Codex: prompt, files, tools, an artifact you can open, then a test. Demonstrations 1, 2, 5, and 6 make the file itself part of the evidence.
:::

---

## A high board score does not mean the model can handle a real patient. {.viz}

![](assets/figures/benchmark_trap.svg){width="100%"}

::: {.viz-explanatory}
The exam is comparable across models, and many of the exam questions are in the training data.

The context of a specific patient, in a specific hospital, and with a specific set of preferences and limitations, will likely always be a challenging application for models.
:::

::: notes
Board-style exams and vendor tables are comparable across models, and many of those items are already in the training data. A real case is a specific patient, in a specific hospital, with a specific set of preferences and limitations — language and cultural context included. That will likely always be a hard job for these models. A high board score does not mean the model can handle weight-based dosing. FDA 2026 paper is still asking how to test open-ended generative AI.
:::

---

## Evidence {background-color="#FF4D00" .section-break}

---

## For real notes, use a hospital-approved cloud or this laptop. {.viz}

![](assets/figures/three_boxes.svg?rev=20260827b){width="100%"}

::: notes
Three places a prompt can live. Consumer ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini send the prompt off-site with no hospital privacy contract. A hospital tool with a business associate agreement is the official cloud path. Laptop Ollama: the vendor never sees the prompt, and they already use that laptop for the EHR. Qwen3.8, Muse Glimmer, and Gemma 4 are examples of local model families, not endorsements or claims that they fit every laptop.
:::

---

## OpenEvidence is a search assistant, not a pediatric guideline. {.viz}

![](assets/figures/artsi_eleven.svg){width="100%"}

::: notes
Artsi 2026 OpenEvidence systematic review. 11 studies, none synthesized as pediatric. The appropriate use they found is guideline-style look-up; it often reinforces rather than changes a plan, and is weaker on complex cases. Not for acting without opening the source. The gray line is the vendor gap: the About page does not name a base model, say whether this is a fine-tuned medical model or a general model with retrieval, or publish a model card. They do advertise in-chat clinical calculators and DeepConsult, a literature agent. Public pages do not describe a coding sandbox. Do not invent LoRA or a GPT version from blogs. End on: search assistant, not pediatric guideline. Company “40% of US physicians” is vendor-reported. Registry: PROSPERO CRD420261289103. Do not invent a pediatric evidence base from 11 adult-leaning studies.
:::

---

## A real citation can still be the wrong answer. {.viz}

![](assets/figures/hajj_counterexample.svg){width="100%"}

::: notes
Hajj inside Artsi: same 15 adult transcatheter tricuspid questions. Bars are the share scored fully accurate by the study’s own definition: ChatGPT-4o 10 of 15 (66.7%) vs OpenEvidence 4 of 15 (26.7%). n=15 is the whole study — gray footer, not a headline. OpenEvidence still cited papers; those citations did not make the answers correct. Do not present it as pediatric. Heuristic: OE for journals, UpToDate for the editorial corpus you already pay for, neither for “what do I do without looking.”
:::

---

## You cannot list a chatbot as an author. AAP has not written a pediatric AI policy. {.viz}

![](assets/figures/settled.svg){width="100%"}

::: notes
As of August 2026. Left column is already in writing: ICMJE January 2026 and COPE 2023 — authors have to be humans who can take responsibility; a chatbot cannot be an author. AMA House of Delegates 10 June 2026 — AI must not replace physician judgment. Right column is what pediatrics still does not have: AAP’s January 2026 digital-ecosystems policy says a dedicated clinical AI statement is forthcoming, so do not invent one; the FDA August 2026 discussion paper is still asking how to test open-ended generative tools; Artsi reviewed 11 OpenEvidence studies and none were synthesized as pediatric. The dated list is still in backup if someone asks.
:::

## Demonstration 5 — Codex repairs the artifact {.nostretch .workshop-text}

::: {.kicker}
Reproduce → repair → test · Codex
:::

::: {.lab-goal}
The provided attendance page looks finished, but typing a week does nothing. Let Codex work on the file itself.
:::

::: {.lab-prompt}
Repair `broken_attendance.html`. Preserve the eight exact counts. Test 4, 1, 8, 9, and blank. No dependencies or network requests.
:::

::: {.lab-steps}
1. Reproduce the failure in the browser.
2. Let Codex inspect and edit the existing file.
3. Enter **4**: one orange bar. Enter **9**: no highlight and a clear message.
:::

::: notes
Prepared folder: /tmp/peds-ai-live-demos/05-repair-page. Open broken_attendance.html before Codex so the room sees the failure. Paste PROMPT.md. Acceptance tests preserve weeks 1–8 and counts 19, 22, 17, 25, 23, 20, 26, 24; valid input highlights one bar; invalid input highlights none and says “Enter a week from 1 to 8”; no external resources; accessible label and live status. Ask whether the failure was data, display, or interaction before revealing the identifier mismatch.
:::

## Demonstration 6 — a fixed packet, a bounded brief {.nostretch .workshop-text}

::: {.kicker}
Synthesize → trace → verify · Codex + three PDFs
:::

::: {.lab-goal}
What should a clinician verify before relying on a clinical AI answer?
:::

::: {.lab-steps}
1. Read the **WHO**, **FDA**, and **Artsi et al.** PDFs only.
2. Build a five-claim evidence table with PDF viewer pages.
3. Distinguish the systematic review from two discussion papers.
4. Ask for a pediatric randomized LP trial: answer **NOT IN PACKET**.
:::

::: notes
Prepared folder: /tmp/peds-ai-live-demos/06-source-packet. Turn web access off and paste PROMPT.md. Exact packet: WHO 2026 discussion paper, DOI 10.2471/B09667; FDA 2026 GenAI-enabled medical devices discussion paper, docket FDA-2026-N-7874; Artsi et al. 2026 OpenEvidence systematic review, DOI 10.1038/s41746-026-03077-4. SOURCE_PACKET.md includes exact filenames and SHA-256 hashes. Open evidence_brief.md, verify one row against the cited PDF viewer page, and read the sentinel answer. None of these is a pediatric trial or clinical guideline.
:::

## Three ways a model is taught: labels, structure, or a score. {.viz}

![](assets/figures/learning_modes.svg){width="100%"}

::: notes
Forty-five seconds if you use it at all. Supervised: x goes with y. Unsupervised: structure, no labels. Reinforcement is a roundabout: try, get scored, nudge, try again. Unlikely to change what they do tomorrow.
:::

---

## Attention is the mix step before the next-token guess. {.viz}

![](assets/figures/attention.svg){width="100%"}

::: notes
Self-attention, 2017. One token looking at the sentence. The main lecture uses the 38.5 °C age example instead.
:::

---

## ChatGPT was the public rupture. o1 made thinking time a product. {.viz}

![](assets/figures/timeline.svg){width="100%"}

::: notes
Full chronology. GPT-2 unsupervised. GPT-3 in-context. InstructGPT RLHF. ChatGPT Nov 2022 is the public rupture. Llama 2 is why a laptop path exists. o1 Sep 2024 is test-time compute as a product. DeepSeek-R1 Jan 2025 showed reasoning-style RL was not OpenAI-only. 2026 names are access classes, not Elo to memorize.
:::

---

## Headline parameter counts are not a quality score. {.viz}

![](assets/figures/param_scale.svg){width="100%"}

::: notes
Parameter counts do not help a resident decide whether to trust an answer. Mixture-of-experts vs dense. Laptop 27-billion and 30-billion models vs trillion-parameter datacenter models. Do not treat the y-axis as quality.
:::

## Judge the claims, not the fluency. {.nostretch .statement-slide}

::: {.copy-block}
**Judge the claims, data, code, and citations—not the fluency or confession.**

ICMJE and *Pediatrics* still ask authors to name the tool. Naming it does not make the science more true.
:::

::: notes
One-line backup, not a second lecture. An adult creatinine in a pediatrics manuscript is a scientific failure, not a missing disclosure checkbox.
:::

## 2026 statements with a public citation, on one line. {.viz}

::: {.kicker}
as of August 2026
:::

![](assets/figures/policy_2026.svg){width="100%"}

::: notes
Walk left to right only if someone asks for names. AAP January: digital-ecosystems policy; the dedicated AI statement is still forthcoming — do not invent one. ICMJE January: name the tool; humans stay accountable. Grundmeier April is a CHOP state-of-the-art review. Bergman JAMA Viewpoint is opinion, not a statute. AMA 10 June: assistive, transparency when models change. FDA August: discussion paper, two-axis risk. WHO B09667: evidence-informed policy for policy-makers, not a pediatric practice guideline.
:::
